name: Olaplex bond builder

lead: Olaplex is a hair-care brand that popularized bond-repair treatments, applied during or after bleaching and coloring. People with bleached or heat-styled hair use it for hair that looks smoother and healthier with less visible damage and breakage.

Its patented ingredient, bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate, is stated by the company to bind keratin and reconnect broken disulfide bonds, which chemical services and heat can sever. The company cites third-party testing, and a 2024 review describes how the ingredient reacts with keratin; the sources reviewed contain no independent clinical trials.

paras: It began as a salon-only step during bleaching and coloring, and later retail products such as the No.3 treatment, No.4 shampoo and No.5 conditioner were added for home use between salon visits.

A 2023 lawsuit by 28 women alleged hair damage and hair loss, and that older Lilial-containing formulas stayed on sale. Olaplex disputes the claims and cites third-party safety testing, and a judge declined class treatment. Cosmetics are not pre-approved by regulators like the US FDA.

angle.text: Olaplex is used by people with bleached or heat-styled hair who want it to look and feel less damaged. The company says its ingredient reconnects broken bonds in the hair, so there is less breakage and the hair looks smoother. The support cited is company testing.

lead: Olaplex is an American hair-care brand founded in 2014 whose products are marketed as repairing hair damaged by chemical, heat and mechanical stress.[1][2] Its products contain a patented ingredient, bis-aminopropyl diglycol dimaleate, which the company says reconnects broken disulfide bonds in hair.[1][2]

The brand launched as a salon-only treatment used during bleaching and coloring, and later added retail products such as the No.3 treatment, No.4 shampoo and No.5 conditioner, creating the broader category of bond-repair or bond-building treatments.[2] Wikipedia notes that a 2024 review of the ingredient describes how it reacts with keratin to restore hair bonds.[1]

Olaplex has also been the subject of litigation, including a trade-secret dispute with L'Oreal and a 2023 lawsuit by women alleging hair damage and hair loss, which the company disputes.[1] No independent clinical trials of bond-builder treatments appear in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Dean and Darcy Christal; chemists Craig Hawker and Eric Pressly[2]
Advent International (2019); public listing 2021; Henkel agreed to acquire in 2026[1]

paras: Hair strength and shape depend partly on disulfide bonds between keratin chains, which bleaching, coloring and chemical services can break. Olaplex's stated approach is to bind to and rebuild these links during and after such services.[2] Product lines include a salon bond-building step, shampoos, conditioners and styling products, and in 2024 the brand introduced bond-shaping technology aimed at curl definition.[2]

According to Grokipedia, the technology was developed in the early 2010s by UC Santa Barbara chemist Craig Hawker and former student Eric Pressly, and the first patent was filed in 2014. Dean Christal built the company around professional salon distribution.[2] Advent International acquired Olaplex in 2019, and the company listed on Nasdaq on September 30, 2021, raising about 1.5 billion US dollars.[1]

Around 2015 Olaplex and L'Oreal discussed a possible takeover that did not proceed; Olaplex later sued over trade secrets, a jury found L'Oreal liable in 2019, the verdict was overturned on appeal, and the companies settled.[1] In 2026 Henkel agreed to acquire the company for about 1.4 billion dollars.[1]

In February 2023, 28 women sued Olaplex alleging that its products damaged hair and caused hair loss, and that older formulas containing Lilial, a chemical considered potentially toxic to reproduction, remained on sale after its removal.[1] Olaplex responded with third-party testing that it says shows its products are safe. By June 2023 a proposed class action had over 100 plaintiffs; a federal judge found the claims too varied for class treatment.[1] Reported effects included hairstylist endorsements, sales and a share-price fall of about 89 percent by the end of 2023.[1]
No studies found. The only research referenced in the sources is a 2024 review of the active ingredient mentioned by Wikipedia, and the company's own third-party safety testing.[1]
